title: Multi-step conversions with dimensional analysis
blurb: Chain unit fractions so the units cancel step by step, and solve two- and three-step conversions across household, metric, weight and time units without guessing which way to go.
question: A child weighs 44 lb, and a medication is ordered at 15 mg per kilogram per day, split into 3 equal doses. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams are in each dose?

teach.h: Let the units do the thinking
teach.body: Formally, dimensional analysis multiplies a quantity by a chain of conversion factors, each written as a fraction equal to 1, so that unwanted units cancel and only the wanted unit remains. In plain English: instead of memorizing whether to multiply or divide, you line up fractions until the units you do not want cross out. It turns a three-step HESI A2 conversion into one tidy line.

teach.h: Wanted unit on top, unwanted unit on the bottom
teach.body: Every factor can be written two ways: 1 tbsp / 3 tsp or 3 tsp / 1 tbsp. Pick the one that puts the unit you are getting rid of on the BOTTOM, so it cancels the same unit on top in the line before. Keep adding factors until only the unit the question asks for is left, then multiply across the top and divide by the bottom.

teach.caption: Repeat moves 2 to 4 for every step in the chain before you compute.

teach.caption: Each fraction equals 1, so multiplying by it changes the unit but never the amount.

teach.h: Worked chains (each line cancels to the wanted unit)
items: 1 pint to tsp: 1 pt × (2 cups / 1 pt) × (8 fl oz / 1 cup) × (2 tbsp / 1 fl oz) × (3 tsp / 1 tbsp) = 96 tsp.
3 ft to cm: 3 ft × (12 in / 1 ft) × (2.54 cm / 1 in) = 91.44 cm.
120 mL/h to mL/min: (120 mL / 1 h) × (1 h / 60 min) = 2 mL/min.
0.3 mg from a vial of 100 mcg per mL: 0.3 mg × (1,000 mcg / 1 mg) × (1 mL / 100 mcg) = 3 mL.
44 lb at 15 mg/kg/day in 3 doses: 44 lb × (1 kg / 2.2 lb) × (15 mg / 1 kg) = 300 mg/day; 300 ÷ 3 = 100 mg per dose.

teach.h: One quart, step by step to milliliters
teach.caption: Every arrow is one unit fraction. A question that wants a quart in milliliters will print the value it expects.

teach.h: Right way up vs upside down
teach.caption: If the units do not cancel, flip the fraction before you calculate.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya checks a liquid dose
teach.body: Priya, a CNA preparing for the HESI A2, sees a 132-lb patient with an order for 2 mg per kilogram of a drug supplied as 40 mg per 5 mL. One chain: 132 lb × (1 kg / 2.2 lb) × (2 mg / 1 kg) × (5 mL / 40 mg). Pounds, kilograms and milligrams cancel: 132 ÷ 2.2 = 60; 60 × 2 = 120; 120 × 5 ÷ 40 = 15 mL. Multiplying by 2.2 instead would have given a dose nearly five times too large.

teach.text: The chain traps: a factor written upside down (so the units multiply instead of cancel), a step left out (cups to fluid ounces skipped), stopping one step short (milligrams when the question asks for milliliters), and, in rates, converting the top unit but forgetting the bottom one (mg per minute left as mg per hour).

items: Write every factor as a fraction equal to 1; the unit to remove goes on the bottom.
Chain as many factors as needed; check that each unit cancels before you multiply.
In a rate (mL/h, mg/min), convert the top unit and the bottom unit separately.
Use memorized factors for spoons, fluid ounces, metric prefixes, 2.2 lb/kg and 2.54 cm/in; use the stem's value for cups, pints, quarts and gallons.
Answer in exactly the unit asked, then sense-check the size.

summary: You can now set up any multi-step conversion as one chain of unit fractions and let the units cancel to the one you want. You can also convert rates and weight-based doses across metric, household, weight and time units in a single line.

A.q: How many tablespoons are in 1 pint?
A.why: 1 pt × (2 cups / 1 pt) × (8 fl oz / 1 cup) × (2 tbsp / 1 fl oz) = 32 tbsp.

whyNot.0: 16 is the number of fluid ounces in a pint; the × 2 step to tablespoons is missing.
whyNot.2: 64 is the number of tablespoons in a quart (2 pints).
whyNot.3: 96 is the number of teaspoons in a pint; it adds an extra × 3 step.

A.q: An infusion runs at 150 mL per hour. What is the rate in milliliters per minute?

whyNot.0: This divides 60 by 150, which gives minutes per milliliter.
whyNot.1: This divides by 100, as if an hour had 100 minutes.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 60; with minutes on top, the hours do not cancel.

A.q: A child is 2 ft 6 in tall. What is the child's height in centimeters, to the nearest tenth?

whyNot.0: This divides 30 by 2.54; the factor is upside down, so inches do not cancel.
whyNot.1: This reads 2 ft 6 in as 26 in (26 × 2.54 = 66.04).
whyNot.3: This reads 2 ft 6 in as 2.6 ft (2.6 × 30.48 = 79.2); 6 in is 0.5 ft.

B.q: A child weighs 44 lb. A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kg per day, split into 3 equal doses. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams are in each dose?

whyNot.1: 300 mg is the daily total; the question asks for one of the 3 doses.
whyNot.2: This skips the conversion and uses 44 lb as if it were kilograms (44 × 15 ÷ 3).
whyNot.3: This multiplies 44 by 2.2 (96.8 kg), the wrong direction.

B.q: A dose of 0.3 mg is ordered. The vial is labeled 100 mcg per mL. How many milliliters should be given?

whyNot.0: This divides 0.3 by 100 without changing milligrams to micrograms.
whyNot.1: This changes 0.3 mg to 30 mcg (× 100) before dividing by 100.
whyNot.3: This changes 0.3 mg to 3,000 mcg (× 10,000) before dividing by 100.

B.q: Using 1 cup = 240 mL, how many liters are in 3 pints?

whyNot.0: This treats a pint as 1 cup (3 × 240 = 720 mL).
whyNot.2: This treats a pint as 4 cups; 4 cups make a quart.
whyNot.3: This divides 1,440 mL by 100 instead of 1,000.

C.q: A patient weighs 154 lb. A drug is ordered at 0.05 mg per kg. The vial contains 500 mcg per mL. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milliliters are needed?

whyNot.0: This changes 3.5 mg to 350 mcg (× 100) before dividing by 500.
whyNot.2: This uses 154 lb as if it were kilograms (7.7 mg = 7,700 mcg).
whyNot.3: This multiplies 154 by 2.2 instead of dividing (338.8 kg).

C.q: A walking program sets a pace of 3 miles per hour. What is this pace in feet per minute?

whyNot.0: 88 ft/min is the pace for 1 mile per hour; the 3 was left out.
whyNot.1: This divides 15,840 by 100, as if an hour had 100 minutes.
whyNot.3: 15,840 is feet per hour; the bottom unit still has to change from hours to minutes.

C.q: A recipe needs 2/3 cup of broth per serving. How many fluid ounces of broth are needed for 9 servings?
C.why: 9 × 2/3 cup = 6 cups. 6 cups × (8 fl oz / 1 cup) = 48 fl oz.

whyNot.0: This uses 4 fl oz per cup, half the true value of 8.
whyNot.1: This takes 2/3 cup as 6 fl oz per serving (9 × 6); 2/3 × 8 = 5 1/3 fl oz.
whyNot.2: This uses 16 fl oz per cup, which is the pint value.

reteach.title: Think of connecting flights
reteach.question: When there is no direct flight, you change planes at one or more hubs. How is a multi-step conversion like a trip with connections?

blocks.h: Each leg has its own ticket
blocks.body: There is no direct flight from pints to teaspoons. You fly pints to cups, cups to fluid ounces, fluid ounces to tablespoons and tablespoons to teaspoons, and each leg needs its own ticket: a unit fraction. You must land in a city before you can leave it, just as each unit must cancel before the next factor uses it. Miss a leg and you never arrive at the right unit.

blocks.text: Skipping a connection is the commonest slip: going straight from cups to tablespoons with × 2 forgets the × 8 leg through fluid ounces.

explain.body: Because 1 g = 1,000 mg, the fractions 1,000 mg / 1 g and 1 g / 1,000 mg both equal 1. Choose the one with the unit you want on top.

test.q: Which unit fraction converts a mass in milligrams to grams?
test.why: Milligrams must cancel, so mg goes on the bottom and g on top: 1 g / 1,000 mg.

whyNot.1: This puts milligrams on top, so they would not cancel; it converts grams to milligrams.
whyNot.2: This fraction is false: 1 mg does not equal 1,000 g.
whyNot.3: This fraction is false: 1,000 g does not equal 1 mg.

explain.body: Line up factors until only the wanted unit is left: 1/2 cup × (8 fl oz / 1 cup) × (2 tbsp / 1 fl oz) × (3 tsp / 1 tbsp).

test.q: How many teaspoons are in 1/2 cup?

whyNot.0: 8 is the number of tablespoons; the × 3 step to teaspoons is missing.
whyNot.1: This uses 3 teaspoons per fluid ounce (4 × 3); 1 fl oz = 6 tsp.
whyNot.3: 48 is the number of teaspoons in a whole cup.

explain.body: In mg per minute, both the top (mg) and the bottom (minute) may need converting. Convert each with its own factor.

test.q: A drug runs at 3 mg per minute. What is the rate in grams per hour?

whyNot.0: This converts the milligrams but leaves the rate per minute (3 mg = 0.003 g).
whyNot.2: This divides 180 mg by 100 instead of 1,000.
whyNot.3: This changes minutes to hours but leaves the 180 in milligrams.

explain.body: Change the weight to kilograms first, then multiply by the dose per kilogram: 66 lb × (1 kg / 2.2 lb) × (5 mg / 1 kg) = 150 mg.

test.q: A 66-lb child is ordered 5 mg of a drug per kg. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams is the dose?

whyNot.0: The setup is right but the decimal point has slipped one place.
whyNot.1: This uses 66 lb as if it were kilograms (66 × 5).
whyNot.2: This multiplies 66 by 2.2 instead of dividing (145.2 kg × 5).
